title: STAT 468 Final Project — Clustering Athlete Aging Curves
text:
Abstract
Athletes reach elite performance at highly variable rates. Some progress rapidly, while others develop more gradually over time. In this project, we model and cluster the rate of progression of Olympic track and field athletes using their aging curves. Unlike team sports, individual sports such as athletics allow for precise comparison through standardized scoring, as individual results are more easily measured in objective terms. To compare athletes across different event disciplines such as jumps and throws, we convert raw performances to a unified scale using the scoring system designed by World Athletics, the world governing body for athletics. 
We apply functional data analysis to smooth each athlete’s aging curve and extract dominant patterns using Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA). Because competition frequency varies by athlete and event, we address irregular and sparse observations using FPCA methods suited for unevenly spaced data.
Clustering the resulting FPCA scores percent change allows us to group athletes based on how fast they improve with age, identifying profiles such as early risers, steady performers, and late bloomers. These clusters provide both descriptive insights into developmental patterns and predictive tools for forecasting when rising athletes might reach elite standards based on early-career data.
This focus on the rate of progression enables a more adaptable and predictive framework allowing coaches, performance analysts, and high performance directors to analyze athletic development.

Traditional aging curve analyses often focus on the average progression or peak age. This approach obscures the diversity in how individuals develop and limits the ability of coaches, scouts, and performance analysts to tailor training and identify untapped potential.
This project addresses that gap by applying functional data analysis and clustering to classify athletes based on the rate and pattern of their performance progression. Rather than examining only final outcomes or single peak performances, the analysis will capture the complete shape of each athlete’s career trajectory from early improvement to peak and subsequent decline.

title: 1  Question
text:
2.1 Introduction
Athlete performance trajectories vary greatly — some athletes achieve elite standards at a young age, while others progress steadily over many years before reaching their peak. Traditional aging curve analyses often focus on the average progression or peak age, which obscures the rich diversity in how individuals develop. This limits the ability of coaches, scouts, and performance analysts to tailor training and identify untapped potential.
This project addresses that gap by applying functional data analysis and clustering to classify athletes based on the rate and pattern of their performance progression. Instead of examining only final outcomes or single peak performances, we aim to capture the shape of each athlete’s career trajectory — from initial improvement to peak and beyond.

title: 1  Question of Interest & Relevance
text:
1.2 Motivation
Understanding the rate of progression provides actionable insights for:
- Coaching: tailoring training loads and peaking strategies to an athlete’s likely development path.
- Talent identification: distinguishing between “late bloomers” who may require patience and “early risers” who peak quickly.
- Long-term planning: projecting when athletes are likely to achieve qualifying standards for major competitions.
By identifying these patterns, organizations can better allocate resources, set realistic performance targets, and make informed selection decisions.

title: 1  Question of Interest & Relevance
text:
1.3 Project Objectives
The main objectives of this project are:

Develop predictive aging curves for individual athletes using observed data points fit with Sparse Functional Principal Component Analysis(FPCA).
Cluster the entire population’s aging curves into three groups based on the rate and shape of progression curve, using the percent change of their IAAF points as the measure of progression dynamics.
Classify existing athletes into meaningful development profiles by matching them to the most representative cluster. Use this classification to estimate when an athlete will achieve a world class standard and to predict their likely development path.

title: 1  Question of Interest & Relevance
text:
1.4 Planned Approach
To achieve these objectives, we will:
- Merge competition results with athlete metadata to create a longitudinal dataset for each athlete and event combination.
- Standardize performance measures (e.g., convert performance results to IAAF points) to allow cross-event comparison.
- Use refund package in R, face.sparse funcion to predict individual’s aging curves.
- Use Sparse Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) to extract dominant patterns in trajectory shapes.
- Apply k-means on sparse FPCA clustering(predicted functions) to group similar progression patterns through the whole population and 7 different event types.
- Interpret and label cluster patterns, and explore predictive assignment for athletes with incomplete career data.
This approach emphasizes progression rate and development patterns rather than absolute performance levels alone. It aims to provide a more dynamic and forward looking view of athlete development that can support practical decision making in competitive sport.

title: 1  Question of Interest & Relevance
text:
2.1 1. Research Questions
Primary question.
How can clustering of functional data classify athletes by the rate and shape of their performance progression across age?
Sub-questions.
1. Can we recover interpretable clusters—e.g., early risers, steady performers, late bloomers—from smoothed age–performance functions?
2. Do clusters meaningfully differ in when and how quickly performance improves, independent of absolute level?
3. Can a partially observed athlete trajectory be mapped to a cluster as an early indicator of future development?
Hypotheses.
- H1: A small number (≈3–5) of functional components explain most between-athlete variability in progression shape.
- H2: Clustering FPCA scores yields profiles with distinct growth-rate signatures.
- H3: Early-career partial curves contain enough shape information to predict profile membership.
Plan.
We will:

Import and tidy historical results and metadata,

Transform to age + standardized performance (IAAF points),

Visualize to check structure and outliers,

Model using Sparse FPCA (face.sparse) and k-means on FPCA scores,

Communicate cluster patterns and a simple mapping of new athletes to clusters.

title: 2  Import
text:
2.2 Data Sources
This project requires three datasets in total. Two datasets will be obtained from WorldAthelete.org and imported with read_csv(). These two datasets contains only the best performance per year for each athlete in each event. That means if an athlete participates in the same event multiple times in a year, only their top result is included. If the same athlete competes in multiple events in the same year, they will have one record for each event. And another iaaf-2005.json dataset is obtained from xxxx’s github and imported with read_json() .

The file career_progression.csv contains performance data, year, date, event, and athlete-link(identifiers).
The file olympics_data.csv provides athlete level metadata including name, birthdate, gender, event, game, game-link, athlete-link, nationality, and Olympic appearances(for example: performance mark and their rank)
The file iaaf-2005.json provides iaaf-points, mark and gender per event

title: 2  Import
text:
2.3 Collection Method
The two athlete related datasets have already been downloaded and imported manually using the standard read-csv() procedure. From “Birthdate” and “Performance date” we will compute the athlete age in years at the time of performance. Age is essential because aging curves are indexed by age rather than by calendar date. Additionally, the iaaf-2005.json dataset is also downloaded and imported manually. We need to convert individual athlete’s performance marks to a standard IAAF-points, so that we can compare their aging curves based on the IAAF-points across different events.

title: 2  Import
text:
2.4 Frequency of Collection
A single collection is sufficient for this study because the focus is historical performance progression. The analysis is not designed for live or streaming updates. Any future extensions that add seasons or events can append to these files and rerun the same pipeline.

title: 2  Import
text:
2.5 Assumptions and Data Preparation Notes
- Athlete age is measured in years using the difference between performance date and birthdate.
- Performance is standardized for cross event comparison using IAAF points.
- Each row in the linked dataset (linked career_progression.csv and olympics_data.csv ) represents one athlete performance on one date for one event. (details in tidy chapter)
- Athlete identifier fields must be consistent across files to enable a reliable merge.
- Basic integrity checks such as duplicate detection and valid date parsing will be performed in the tidy chapter.

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.1.1 Justification of Methods
The join is necessary to ensure all performance marks are converted to a standardized IAAF points scale, enabling meaningful comparison of athletes across different events. Using only records with valid birthdate and performance date ensures that the computed age is accurate, which is essential for aligning performances on the aging curve.
Parsing dates and calculating age at this stage simplifies downstream analysis, because all modeling steps can use a consistent age variable without re-computation.
Restricting each athlete to their best performance per year per event eliminates multiple highly correlated entries for the same individual, reducing redundancy and ensuring that the aging curve reflects peak ability in each season.


3.1.2 Relevant Unit Tests

Test 1: Check that the join produces no duplicate athlete-event-year records.

Test 2: Verify that every record has a valid non-missing IAAF points value after the join.

Test 3: Confirm that all age_years values are positive and fall within a reasonable range (e.g., 10 to 60).

Test 4: Check that the number of unique athlete IDs matches across the original and linked datasets.

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.2 Data Filtering
Records lacking a valid birthdate or performance date were removed, as these fields are essential for calculating the athlete’s age at performance. Both dates were parsed into date objects, and age in years and in days was computed. The dataset preserves only one row per athlete per event per year, consistent with the fact that the source files already contain only the single best performance per year for each athlete–event combination. If an athlete competed in multiple events in the same year, each event is treated as a separate aging curve.

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.3 Rationale
Merging the datasets at this stage ensures that all records are standardized to IAAF points before modeling. Removing incomplete records avoids downstream errors in age calculation. Using only season-best performances reduces redundancy, limits within-year correlation, and focuses the analysis on peak capability for each season.

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.1.1 Step 1: Clean Olympics_data.csv Data
The Olympic dataset is imported and cleaned to provide athlete-level metadata. Key transformations include:
Standardized column names using janitor::clean_names()
Parsed competition dates into start and end
Separated gender from event name
Removed wheelchair events
Manually corrected birthdate for Aminata CAMARA
Standardized gender labels (“Men’s” → “Men”, etc.)
Converted date strings to Date objects
Calculated athlete age at the time of competition
Created ordered factor for Olympic Games
Classified events into types (e.g., Sprints, Throws) and categories (Track vs. Field)
Standardized event names (e.g., merged “Javelin Throw (old)” with “Javelin Throw”)
Extracted competition year from the end date Code shows below:

Olympics_data <- read_csv("/Users/yushiliu/Stat 468 final project/data/track and field data/olympics_data.csv", show_col_types = F) %>%
  janitor::clean_names() %>% 
  separate_wider_delim(date, delim = "–", names = c("start", "end")) %>%
  separate_wider_delim(cols = event, names = c("gender", "event"), delim = " ",
                           too_many = "merge") %>%
  filter(str_detect(event, "Wheelchair", negate = T)) %>% 
  mutate(
        # Manually fixed Aminata CAMARA's age
    birth_date = if_else(name == "Aminata CAMARA", "06 DEC 1973", birth_date),
    gender = if_else(gender == "Men's", "Men", "Women"),
    across(c(birth_date, end),  ~as.Date(format(
    as.Date(., format = "%d %b %Y"), "%Y-%m-%d"))),
    age = year(end) - year(birth_date),
         games = factor(games, ordered = T,
                        levels = c("The XXXII Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXXI Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXX Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXIX Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXVIII Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXVII Olympic Games",
                                   "The XXVI Olympic Games"
                        ),
                        labels = c("Tokyo '20", "Rio '16", "London '12", 
                                   "Beijing '08", "Athens '04", "Sydney '00",
                                   "Atlanta '96")),
    event_type = case_match(
      event,
      c("100 Metres", "200 Metres", "400 Metres", "400 Metres Hurdles", "100 Metres Hurdles", "110 Metres Hurdles") ~ "Sprints",
      c("800 Metres", "1500 Metres", "3000 Metres Steeplechase") ~ "Middle Distance",
      c("5000 Metres", "10,000 Metres") ~ "Long Distance",
      c("Heptathlon", "Decathlon") ~ "Combined Events",
      c("High Jump", "Long Jump", "Triple Jump", "Pole Vault") ~ "Jumps",
      c("Shot Put", "Discus Throw", "Hammer Throw", "Javelin Throw", "Javelin Throw (old)") ~ "Throws",
      c("10 Kilometres Race Walk", "20 Kilometres Race Walk", "50 Kilometres Race Walk", "Marathon") ~ "Road Races",
      .default = "Other"
    ),
         event_category = if_else(str_detect(event, "Metres|Walk|Wheelchair") |event %in% c("Marathon"), "Track", "Field")
         ) %>% 
  mutate(event = if_else(event == "Javelin Throw (old)", "Javelin Throw", event),
         games_year = year(end)) %>% rename("nationality" = nat)

The result is a clean metadata table named Olympics_data.


3.1.2 Step 2: Clean Career Progression Data and merge with Olympic dataset
The career progression dataset is imported and cleaned to provide yearly performance records. Key steps include:

Removed duplicate rows
Parsed performance dates
Flagged retired athletes based on last recorded year
Calculated training age as years since first appearance, grouped by athlete and event

This produces a clean performance table named Career_progression. We then merge Career_progression with Olympics_data using athlete_link and event. This creates a unified dataset containing both performance records and athlete metadata. After the join, we compute:
-Age at performance:
age_years: Year of performance minus year of birth
age_days: Exact age in days using difftime(date, birth_date)
-Cleaned performance string: Removed hand-timing flags
-Numeric mark:
Track events: Time in seconds
Field events: Distance or height
-Season best indicator:
Track: Minimum time
Field: Maximum distance/height
-Percent off peak: Deviation from season best within athlete and event
-Olympic year flag: Based on season year
-Tie resolution: Within each athlete-event-year group, keep the record with the largest age in days
This final cleaned dataset is saved as athlete_bests.

# load career progression data and identify athletes who are still active
Career_progression <- read_csv("/Users/yushiliu/Stat 468 final project/data/track and field data/career_progression (2).csv", show_col_types = F) %>% 
  distinct() |> 
  mutate(date = parse_date_time(date, orders = c("%d %b %Y", "%d-%b-%y"))) %>%
  mutate(retired = if_else(max(year) <= 2022, T, F),
         training_age = year - min(year) + 1,
         .by = c("athlete_link", "event")) 

# find the seasons best performances of each athlete
athlete_bests <-
  Career_progression %>%  inner_join(
    Olympics_data %>%  filter(!is.na(birth_date)) %>%
      distinct(birth_date, athlete_links, event, event_type, .keep_all = T) %>%
      select(name, birth_date, athlete_links, event, nationality, event_type, 
             event_category, gender, games_year),
    by = c("athlete_link" = "athlete_links", "event")
  ) %>%  
  mutate(age_years = year(date) - year(birth_date), 
         age_days = as.double(
           difftime(
             date, birth_date,units = "days"
           )
         ),
         performance = str_remove_all(performance, "h") # I will count hand timed results as legitimate
         ) %>%
    mutate(mark = if_else(
      event_category == "Track",
      as.numeric(
        difftime(
          lubridate::parse_date_time2(performance, orders = c("%H:%M:%S", "%M:%S:00", "%M:%OS", "%OS"), exact = T),
          lubridate::parse_date_time2("0", orders ="S"),
          units = "secs"
        )
      ), parse_number(performance)),
      # the below accounts for edge cases that lubridate can't parse, like a 62s 400MH
      mark = if_else(is.na(mark), parse_number(performance), mark)
      ) %>%
    mutate(
      best_performance = case_when(
        event_category == "Track" & mark == min(mark, na.rm = T) ~ T, # we want the lowest time
        event_category == "Field" & mark == max(mark, na.rm = T) ~ T, # we want the furthest/highest performance
        .default = F
      ),
      percent_off_peak = if_else(event_category == "Track", abs((mark - min(mark, na.rm = T))/mark), 
                                 abs((mark - max(mark, na.rm = T))/mark)),
      olympic_year = if_else(year %in% c(seq(1980, 2016, 4), 2021), T, F),
      .by = c("athlete_link", "event")
    ) %>% 
   # remove duplicate seasons bests
  slice_max(with_ties = F, n = 1, order_by = age_days, by = c("event", "year",  "athlete_link"))



3.1.3 Step 3: Join with IAAF Points
We import the IAAF scoring table from iaaf-2025.json, flattening it into a tibble with: gender, event, mark and points.
To ensure compatibility, we create a copy of athlete_bests named athlete_bests_clean with:
-gender converted to lowercase
-event names standardized to match IAAF naming conventions (e.g., “100 Metres” → “100m”, “110 Metres Hurdles” → “110mH”)
We then join athlete_bests_clean to iaaf_table using a nearest match on mark, grouped by gender and event. This assigns an IAAF points value to each season-best record.
-The join uses closest(mark <= mark) to find the nearest valid score
-Missing points are replaced with 0 to avoid downstream errors
-The final dataset is stored as athlete_bests_points
The cleaned athlete bests dataset from the Import section was merged with the IAAF points table (iaaf-2005.json) to attach standardized scoring. Event names were harmonized between sources (e.g., "100 Metres" → "100m", "110 Metres Hurdles" → "110mH", "Marathon" → "Road Marathon").
The join was performed on gender and event using the nearest mark in the IAAF table, ensuring each record received the closest possible standardized points value. Merge to one row per athlete–event–date.

athlete_bests <- readRDS("data/athlete_bests.rds")
raw_json <- read_json("data/track and field data/iaaf-2025.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

# Convert list of lists to a flat tibble
iaaf_table <- tibble::tibble(
  gender = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "gender"),
  event = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "event"),
  mark = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "mark"),
  points = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "points")
)
athlete_bests_clean <- athlete_bests |> 
  mutate(
    gender = tolower(gender),
    event = case_when(
      event == "100 Metres" ~ "100m",
      event == "200 Metres" ~ "200m",
      event == "400 Metres" ~ "400m",
      event == "800 Metres" ~ "800m",
      event == "1500 Metres" ~ "1500m",
      event == "5000 Metres" ~ "5000m",
      event == "10,000 Metres" ~ "10000m",
      event == "Marathon" ~ "Road Marathon",
      event == "Triple Jump" ~ "TJ",
      event == "Long Jump" ~ "LJ",
      event == "High Jump" ~ "HJ",
      event == "Shot Put" ~ "SP",
      event == "Discus Throw" ~ "DT",
      event == "Hammer Throw" ~ "HT",
      event == "Javelin Throw" ~ "JT",
      event == "Decathlon" ~ "Dec.",
      event == "Heptathlon" ~ "Hept.",
      event == "Pole Vault" ~ "PV",
      event == "10 Kilometres Race Walk" ~ "10,000mW",
      event == "50 Kilometres Race Walk" ~ "50,000mW",
      event == "20 Kilometres Race Walk" ~ "20,000mW",
      event == "100 Metres Hurdles" ~ "100mH",
      event == "110 Metres Hurdles" ~ "110mH",
      event == "400 Metres Hurdles" ~ "400mH",
      event == "3000 Metres Steeplechase" ~ "3000m SC",
      TRUE ~ event
    )
  )

# join iaaf_table with athlete_bests and get full dataset with result points
round_decimals <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  round(x * 10^digits) / 10^digits}

athlete_bests_points <- 
  athlete_bests_clean |>
    left_join(iaaf_table, join_by(gender, event, closest(mark <= mark))) |> 
  replace_na(list(points = 0))

title: 3  Tidy
section: 3.4 What is taken in from Import
text:
3.4 What is taken in from Import
One dataset named Olympics_data that already has clean names, parsed dates, gender and event split, wheelchair records removed, one manual birth date fix, standardized gender text, an ordered factor for Games, derived event type and a track or field category, a unified javelin name, and the Games year.

One table named Career_progression that already has duplicates removed, parsed performance dates, a retired flag by athlete and event, and training age by athlete and event.

title: 3  Tidy
section: 3.5 Merge to build season bests with ages and numeric marks
text:
3.5 Merge to build season bests with ages and numeric marks
Career_progression is inner joined to Olympics_data using athlete link and event.

After the join the following variables are created.

Age in years at performance from the year of performance minus the year of birth.

Age in days at performance from the difference between performance date and birth date.

A cleaned performance string with hand timing flag removed.

A numeric mark that is time in seconds for track and a numeric distance or height for field.

A season best indicator that selects the minimum time for track and the maximum distance or height for field within each athlete and event.

Percent off peak computed within each athlete and event using the record specific mark relative to the best mark.

An Olympic year indicator based on the season year.

Within each athlete, event, and year grouping, a single record is kept by taking the row with the largest age in days to resolve ties.

The result is saved as athlete_bests and written to disk as an rds file.

title: 3  Tidy
section: 3.6 Ingest the IAAF points reference and harmonize event names
text:
3.6 Ingest the IAAF points reference and harmonize event names
The file iaaf-2025.json is read, flattened, and turned into a tibble with four columns: gender, event, mark, and points.

A copy of athlete_bests named athlete_bests_clean is created with gender forced to lower case and with event names standardized to match the IAAF naming used in the json. For example 100 Metres becomes 100m, 110 Metres Hurdles becomes 110mH.

title: 3  Tidy
section: 3.7 Attach standardized points to season bests
text:
3.7 Attach standardized points to season bests
The table athlete_bests_clean is left joined to iaaf_table by gender and event using a nearest rule on mark via the closest helper. This assigns an IAAF points value to each season best record. Any missing points produced by the join are replaced with zero so that downstream code does not error on missing values. The result is stored as athlete_bests_points.

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.3 Why these choices are appropriate
Joining before modeling ensures that every observation is on a common comparable scale.

Standardizing event names before the join prevents many to one and failed matches.

Keeping one season best per athlete and event per year preserves the longitudinal shape while avoiding within season duplication.

Numeric mark construction respects the measurement scale of track and field. Times are in seconds while field marks remain in their numeric distance or height.

The nearest rule attaches the appropriate IAAF score for the observed mark with minimal interpolation.

  event = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "event"),
  mark = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "mark"),
  points = sapply(raw_json, `[[`, "points")
)
athlete_bests_clean <- athlete_bests |> 
  mutate(
    gender = tolower(gender),
    event = case_when(
      event == "100 Metres" ~ "100m",
      event == "200 Metres" ~ "200m",
      event == "400 Metres" ~ "400m",
      event == "800 Metres" ~ "800m",
      event == "1500 Metres" ~ "1500m",
      event == "5000 Metres" ~ "5000m",
      event == "10,000 Metres" ~ "10000m",
      event == "Marathon" ~ "Road Marathon",
      event == "Triple Jump" ~ "TJ",
      event == "Long Jump" ~ "LJ",
      event == "High Jump" ~ "HJ",
      event == "Shot Put" ~ "SP",
      event == "Discus Throw" ~ "DT",
      event == "Hammer Throw" ~ "HT",
      event == "Javelin Throw" ~ "JT",
      event == "Decathlon" ~ "Dec.",
      event == "Heptathlon" ~ "Hept.",
      event == "Pole Vault" ~ "PV",
      event == "10 Kilometres Race Walk" ~ "10,000mW",
      event == "50 Kilometres Race Walk" ~ "50,000mW",
      event == "20 Kilometres Race Walk" ~ "20,000mW",
      event == "100 Metres Hurdles" ~ "100mH",
      event == "110 Metres Hurdles" ~ "110mH",
      event == "400 Metres Hurdles" ~ "400mH",
      event == "3000 Metres Steeplechase" ~ "3000m SC",
      TRUE ~ event
    )
  )

# join iaaf_table with athlete_bests and get full dataset with result points
round_decimals <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  round(x * 10^digits) / 10^digits}

athlete_bests_points <- 
  athlete_bests_clean |>
    left_join(iaaf_table, join_by(gender, event, closest(mark <= mark))) |> 
  replace_na(list(points = 0))

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.2 Why This Pipeline Works
-Sequential cleaning ensures each dataset is tidy before merging
-Joining Olympic and career data first preserves athlete-event-year structure
-Standardizing event names before scoring avoids mismatches
-One season-best per athlete-event-year maintains longitudinal integrity
-Numeric mark construction respects measurement scale:
Track: time in seconds
Field: distance or height
-Nearest match rule minimizes interpolation error when assigning IAAF scores

title: 3  Tidy
text:
3.4 Notes on join Behaviour
Your join uses closest on a condition with mark on both sides. That requires a recent dplyr and depends on how the IAAF reference orders marks. If you ever observe mismatched points at event boundaries, consider switching to an explicit directional rule that treats track and field differently, where track uses the largest IAAF mark that is less than or equal to the observed time and field uses the smallest IAAF mark that is greater than or equal to the observed distance or height.
The closest() join on mark requires a recent version of dplyr. If mismatches occur near event boundaries, consider refining the logic:
Track events: Use the largest IAAF mark ≤ observed time
Field events: Use the smallest IAAF mark ≥ observed distance
This directional rule ensures accurate scoring near performance thresholds.
